message.content:
Below is a concise overview of the key rights and protections you have as a tenant in Texas. These rights are derived from the Texas Property Code, local ordinances, and general landlord‑tenant law. Keep in mind that specific situations (e.g., lease terms, local city ordinances) may add additional rules. | Category | What You’re Entitled To | Practical Tips | |----------|------------------------|----------------| | **Security Deposit** | • Landlord may charge up to **one month’s rent** for a furnished unit and **two months’ rent** for an unfurnished unit.
• Must be returned within **30 days** after you move out, minus any lawful deductions. | • Get a written receipt and keep a copy of the lease.
• Inspect the unit with the landlord before moving out and document any damage. | | **Habitability** | • Landlord must maintain the premises in a safe, sanitary condition (e.g., plumbing, heating, electrical).
• Must repair or replace broken fixtures, pipes, or appliances that affect health or safety. | • Report problems in writing (email or letter) and keep copies.
• If repairs aren’t made within a reasonable time, you may withhold rent or pursue a repair‑and‑deduct remedy. | | **Rent Payment & Late Fees** | • Rent is due on the date specified in the lease.
• Landlord may charge a late fee only if it’s stated in the lease and is **reasonable** (usually not more than 5% of the monthly rent). | • Pay on time or negotiate a payment plan if you’re having trouble. | | **Right to Quiet Enjoyment** | • Landlord cannot enter your unit without **reasonable notice** (typically 24 hours) unless it’s an emergency. | • Keep a log of any unannounced entries. | | **Privacy & Entry** | • Landlord must give **reasonable notice** (usually 24–48 hours) before entering, except in emergencies. | • Ask for a written notice if you suspect an unauthorized entry. | | **Discrimination** | • Landlords cannot discriminate based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, disability, familial status, or source of income (e.g., public assistance). | • File a complaint with the Texas Commission on Human Rights if you suspect discrimination. | | **Lease Termination** | • Either party may terminate a lease with proper notice (usually 30 days for month‑to‑month agreements).
• Landlord must provide a written notice of termination. | • Keep a copy of any termination notice. | | **Repair‑and‑Deduct** | • If the landlord fails to fix a habitability issue, you may repair it yourself and deduct the cost from your rent, but you must follow the correct procedure (e.g., give notice, keep receipts). | • Document all communications and keep receipts. | | **Rent Increase** | • For month‑to‑month leases, landlords must give **30 days’ notice** before raising rent. | • Review your lease for any rent‑increase clauses. | | **Eviction Process** | • Landlord must serve a **notice** (e.g., 3‑day notice for nonpayment, 30‑day notice for lease violation).
• Eviction can only proceed through the court system. | • Respond promptly to notices; consider negotiating a payment plan or settlement. | | **Security Deposit Deductions** | • Landlord may deduct for unpaid rent, damages beyond normal wear and tear, or cleaning costs if the unit isn’t left in a clean condition. | • Request an itemized list of deductions if you disagree. | | **Legal Remedies** | • You can file a claim in small‑claims court for unpaid security deposit or damages. | • Keep all documentation (photos, receipts, correspondence). | ### How to Protect Your Rights 1. **Read Your Lease Carefully** – All terms, including rent amount, security deposit limits, and notice periods, should be spelled out in writing. 2. **Document Everything** – Photos, videos, emails, and written notices help prove your case if disputes arise. 3. **Know Local Ordinances** – Some cities (e.g., Austin, Dallas) have additional tenant protections, such as rent control or eviction moratoriums. 4. **Seek Legal Advice** – If you’re facing eviction or a dispute over a deposit, consult a tenant‑rights attorney or a local legal aid organization. 5. **File Complaints** – If you believe your landlord is violating Texas law, you can file a complaint with the Texas Commission on Human Rights or the Texas Attorney General’s office. --- #### Quick Reference Checklist - [ ] Lease signed and dated - [ ] Security deposit receipt - [ ] Move‑in inspection checklist - [ ] Written notice of any repairs needed - [ ] Copies of all correspondence with landlord - [ ] Documentation of any damage or repairs If you have a specific situation (e.g., a notice of eviction, a dispute over a deposit, or a repair request), let me know and I can give more tailored advice or draft a letter you might send to your landlord.
